presidents.name: James K. Polk
trivia: First sitting president widely credited with posing for a photograph while in office.
First successful “dark horse” presidential nominee—little-known nationally when Democrats chose him in 1844.
Campaigned on serving only one term and kept that promise.
Achieved his four stated goals: lower tariffs, restore the Independent Treasury, settle Oregon, and gain California/Southwest land.
President during the Mexican–American War, which added vast territory including California.
His supporters’ slogan “Fifty-four Forty or Fight!” demanded a northern Oregon border at latitude 54°40′.
Added more square miles to the U.S. than any president except Jefferson.
Died just three months after leaving office—the shortest post-presidency of anyone who left voluntarily.
Known as a workaholic who personally managed wartime details and rarely vacationed.
First Lady Sarah Polk banned dancing and hard liquor from White House social events.
Pub-trivia shorthand: one-term workhorse who wins the Mexican–American War and adds California.

presidents.name: Zachary Taylor
trivia: First career Army general elected president who had never held elected office; nicknamed “Old Rough and Ready.”
Became a national hero as a commander in the Mexican–American War.
Second president to die in office, after only about 16 months.
Owned enslaved people but opposed letting slavery expand into new western territories.
In 1991 his body was exhumed to test a poisoning theory; tests did not support arsenic poisoning.
Never cast a presidential ballot before running himself—army life kept him out of party politics.
Didn’t learn he had been nominated for weeks because mail was slow to reach his Louisiana home.
His daughter Sarah Knox Taylor married Jefferson Davis, who later became Confederate president.
His favorite war horse, Old Whitey, was sometimes allowed to graze on the White House lawn.
As a Whig president, he angered both Northern and Southern factions over how to handle slavery in new lands.
Pub-trivia shorthand: “Old Rough and Ready”—Mexican War hero who dies early in office; Fillmore replaces him.

presidents.name: Millard Fillmore
trivia: Last president from the Whig Party.
Became president when Zachary Taylor died in 1850.
Signed the Compromise of 1850, including the Fugitive Slave Act requiring return of escaped enslaved people.
Ran for president again in 1856 as the Know-Nothing (American Party) nominee.
Started a formal White House library with books purchased for the mansion.
Turned down an honorary degree from Oxford, saying he had not done enough to deserve a literary honor he hadn’t earned.
Born in a log cabin in New York’s Finger Lakes region.
Did not meet his running mate Zachary Taylor until after they won the 1848 election.
His administration launched Commodore Matthew Perry’s expedition that forced Japan to open to U.S. trade.
A self-taught, then formally trained lawyer who rose through Buffalo, New York politics.
Pub-trivia shorthand: the forgotten president after Taylor who signs the Compromise of 1850; last Whig.

presidents.name: Franklin Pierce
trivia: Only president from New Hampshire.
Youngest person elected president up to that time (age 48).
Signed the Kansas–Nebraska Act (1854), which let settlers vote on slavery and sparked “Bleeding Kansas” violence.
Days before inauguration, his 11-year-old son Benjamin was killed when their train derailed.
College friend of author Nathaniel Hawthorne, who wrote Pierce’s 1852 campaign biography.
Served as a brigadier general in the Mexican–American War.
Nicknamed “Young Hickory of the Granite Hills,” linking him to Andrew Jackson and New Hampshire’s nickname.
Democrats refused to renominate the sitting president in 1856.
Often ranked among the least successful presidents for failing to stop the slide toward civil war.
Struggled with heavy drinking and depression after family deaths, which damaged his public standing.
Pub-trivia shorthand: Kansas–Nebraska / “Bleeding Kansas” president; only one from New Hampshire.

presidents.name: James Buchanan
trivia: Only U.S. president who never married; his niece Harriet Lane served as White House hostess.
Last president born in the 1700s (1791).
While he was still in office after Lincoln’s 1860 win, seven Southern states seceded; he argued he lacked power to stop them.
Welcomed the Supreme Court’s Dred Scott ruling, which said Congress could not ban slavery in the territories and that Black Americans could not be citizens.
Usually finishes at or near the bottom of historians’ presidential rankings.
Before the presidency he was secretary of state and U.S. minister to both Russia and Britain.
Democrats nominated him in 1856 partly because, as minister to Britain, he had been overseas during the violent Kansas fights and looked like a safer national choice.
Tried to admit Kansas as a slave state under the pro-slavery Lecompton Constitution; Congress rejected that path.
Hoped to be remembered as the leader who preserved the Union, then watched it break apart on his watch.
Immediate predecessor of Abraham Lincoln—often the answer to “who was president just before the Civil War?”
Pub-trivia shorthand: the guy right before Lincoln—bachelor president as the Union starts falling apart.

presidents.name: Abraham Lincoln
trivia: First Republican elected president.
First president assassinated: shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford’s Theatre on April 14, 1865.
Issued the Emancipation Proclamation (1863) and pushed the 13th Amendment abolishing slavery.
Led the Union through the Civil War and gave the Gettysburg Address.
Tallest U.S. president, about 6 feet 4 inches.
Only U.S. president to hold a patent—he invented a device to lift riverboats over shallow shoals.
Grew his famous beard after an 1860 letter from 11-year-old Grace Bedell urged him to, saying it would improve his looks.
Mostly self-educated lawyer who grew up in Kentucky, Indiana, and Illinois cabin country.
Won reelection in 1864 with Democrat Andrew Johnson on a temporary “National Union” ticket.
Suspended habeas corpus during the Civil War so the government could jail suspected Confederate sympathizers without trial.
Pub-trivia shorthand: Civil War president; Emancipation; Gettysburg Address; first assassinated president.

presidents.name: Andrew Johnson
trivia: First president impeached by the House of Representatives; the Senate acquitted him by a single vote.
Only former president later elected to the U.S. Senate.
Took office after Lincoln’s assassination; as a Tennessee senator he was the only Southern senator who stayed loyal to the Union.
Could not read or write until adulthood; his wife Eliza taught him.
Fought Radical Republicans over Reconstruction and vetoed major civil rights and Freedmen’s Bureau bills.
A Tennessee Democrat put on Lincoln’s 1864 ticket to attract War Democrats and border-state voters.
Worked as a tailor in Greeneville, Tennessee before entering politics.
Was visibly drunk when sworn in as vice president in March 1865—a public embarrassment.
Impeached mainly for firing Secretary of War Edwin Stanton in violation of the Tenure of Office Act.
Not the same person as Lyndon B. Johnson (LBJ)—Andrew Johnson was president in the 1860s.
Pub-trivia shorthand: Lincoln’s accidental successor; first impeached president; fights Reconstruction Republicans.

presidents.name: Ulysses S. Grant
trivia: First West Point graduate elected president.
As Union general-in-chief, accepted Robert E. Lee’s surrender at Appomattox Court House (1865).
Youngest person elected president up to that time (age 46).
Appears on the $50 bill.
Born Hiram Ulysses Grant; “Ulysses S. Grant” stuck after a West Point enrollment error, and he kept it.
His two terms were hit by scandals like the Whiskey Ring, though Grant himself was not shown to be personally stealing.
Used federal force against the Ku Klux Klan during Reconstruction.
Finished his Personal Memoirs while dying of throat cancer; Mark Twain’s firm published them and rescued Grant’s family from debt.
Failed as a farmer and businessman in the 1850s before the Civil War made him famous.
Smoked constantly; after early Civil War victories, admirers mailed him so many cigars that he was said to go through about 20 a day.
Pub-trivia shorthand: Appomattox general → president; $50 bill; scandal-plagued Reconstruction years.

presidents.name: Rutherford B. Hayes
trivia: First president to have a telephone installed in the White House; the number was simply “1.”
Won the disputed 1876 election after losing the popular vote, decided by the Compromise of 1877.
Ended Reconstruction by withdrawing the last federal troops from the South as part of that 1877 settlement.
Promised to serve only one term and did not run again.
First Lady Lucy Hayes banned alcohol at White House events and was nicknamed “Lemonade Lucy.”
The Compromise of 1877 is often summarized as: Hayes becomes president, Southern Democrats regain control of their state governments.
A Civil War general who was wounded several times and rose to brevet major general.
Associated with beginning the annual White House Easter Egg Roll on the mansion grounds.
Republican from Ohio during a stretch when Ohio produced several presidents.
Full name Rutherford Birchard Hayes—middle name Birchard.
Pub-trivia shorthand: wins the stolen-feeling 1876 election; ends Reconstruction; first White House phone.
quiz: Which president had the first telephone installed in the White House?

presidents.name: James A. Garfield
trivia: Only sitting member of the House of Representatives ever elected president.
Presidency lasted about six months; shot by Charles Guiteau and died 80 days later from complications.
Last president born in a log cabin.
According to contemporary accounts, he could write Latin with one hand and Greek with the other at the same time.
Had been president of Hiram College and a Civil War major general before Congress.
Inventor Alexander Graham Bell tried an early metal detector to locate the bullet in Garfield’s body but failed, partly because of metal bed springs.
Assassin Charles Guiteau was a rejected office-seeker who claimed God ordered the shooting.
Public anger over the assassination helped pass civil service reform under successor Chester A. Arthur.
Another Ohio Republican in the late-1800s run of Ohio-born presidents.
Doctors repeatedly probed the wound with unsterile instruments; infection likely contributed as much as the bullet to his death.
Pub-trivia shorthand: brilliant short-timers’ president—assassinated after months; his death forces civil-service reform.
quiz: Which president did Alexander Graham Bell try to help with an early metal detector?
